k-1.x_notes: Six problems, each with a clean actual-size board. Covering shapes with blues (the 8-triangle trapezoid is impossible because it has 5 up-triangles and 3 down), fewest greens in triangles of side 2, 3 and 4, find-all on hexagons, fewest blocks of any kind (the side-3 triangle can be done with 3 trapezoids), a blue-block placement game whose answers come out first, second, first, first, second, and the 6 tilings of a 2-1-2 hexagon. The shared rules include 'Use only the small blocks', which matters because the P4 shapes are exactly the 3x triangle, 2x rhombus and 2x trapezoid, and the upscale blocks are in the room. P6 gives six full-size boards, so children build and compare every tiling with real blocks and draw nothing. Weaknesses: P3 and P6 print exactly as many boards as there are tilings (2+3 and 6), which gives away how many to find, and P6 needs about 48 blue blocks.
k-1.y_notes: Same five opening problems with the same correct boards and answers. P5 asks children to circle the words first or second, which is fine but harder for a kindergartner to read than X's 1/2. P3 prints one more board than there are tilings (3 hexagons for 2, 4 elongated hexagons for 3), and P6 uses one big building board plus 8 small drawing boards for 6 tilings. Neither gives away the count, and the small boards follow the 'compact when recording' guidance. But drawing rhombus tilings on half-inch triangles is a fine-motor strain for K, and an empty leftover board can confuse children or a non-mathematician helper. The rules never exclude the upscale blocks, so each P4 shape and the P1 parallelogram can be covered by one big block.
k-1.reason: The mathematics is identical. X closes the upscale-block loophole that trivializes P4 and keeps P6 fully hands-on, which outweighs Y's better choice not to reveal tiling counts through the number of boards.

grades-2-3.x_notes: This is a strong coloring-obstruction sequence, and Y has the same one. Possible and impossible boards include the balanced but disconnected hourglass F and the trapezoid C, which has an even number of triangles but more up- than down-triangles. P3 asks for the fewest greens in triangles of side 2 to 5, with a proof for the biggest. P4 generalizes to 10 and 100. P5 asks whether purple chevrons can ever beat blues, P6 asks children to invent a 20-triangle board that forces 6 greens, and P7 asks which positions for two greens on a side-2 hexagon work. A brute-force check confirms the 'one up and one down' rule is exact. X adds 'Use only the small blocks', which matters because a 2x or 3x green would wreck the fewest-greens counts. P3 says 'on this page and the next', which ties the side-5 triangle on page 4 to the problem. P4 asks why nobody can do better for side 10. P7 asks children to explain why the other placements fail, which is the age-appropriate direction.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Pages, boards and answers are the same as X's. It does not exclude the upscale blocks. P3 does not mention that the side-5 triangle is on the next page, so a child may not connect page 4, which has no problem number, to P3. P4 asks only for the numbers, without the general lower-bound argument. P7 says 'explain why your rule is right', which also asks for sufficiency, a harder proof for this age. Otherwise it is equally sound.
grades-2-3.reason: The packets are almost identical. X's small clarifications (small blocks only, the page-4 continuation, and the impossibility explanation in P4) make it slightly more self-running.

grades-4-5.x_notes: A well-built kernel-2 arc. It finds the 6 tilings of a 1-2-2 hexagon, defines flips and builds the flip graph, then asks for the fewest flips between pairs on the side-2 hexagon. I verified the A-B, C-D and E-F distances as 3, 4 and 8. P4 asks for a 4-flip round trip from A, which exists, and asks whether 5 or 7 are possible (no, by parity). Ribbons follow, with a correct LRRLR example, then a parity proof, a lower bound for E to F, counting all 20 tilings, and counting the 20 tilings of a 1-3-3 hexagon. In P2 children number their P1 drawings and draw the graph in open space, with no recopying. P4 gives five small hexagons to record the cycle, and P7 allows listing tilings as ribbons. Weaknesses: the P3 target pictures keep faint grid lines inside each rhombus, which makes them busier to read, and pages 4 and 5 have a lot of unused space.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Same problems with correct mathematics. The P3 target pictures are clean rhombi and easier to read. But P2 makes children redraw all six P1 coverings on fixed small boards before drawing graph edges between them. That is copying busywork, and the edges must squeeze between pictures in a 2x4 grid. P4 ('any covering') leaves only two lines and no boards for recording the flip cycle. Some starting coverings, E and F, admit no such 4-cycle, so a child who starts there will be stuck. The rules do not exclude the upscale blocks.
grades-4-5.reason: The mathematics and sequence are the same. X's workspace choices (no redrawing in P2, recording boards and a known-good starting covering in P4) serve the work better than Y's cleaner P3 pictures.

overall.reason: Both packets come from the same design. They have identical, correct and well-developed problems in every band, so the differences are small. X is consistently a little more robust in the room: it excludes the upscale blocks that would trivialize several counting problems, keeps the K-1 work fully hands-on, avoids redrawing busywork in grades 4-5, and gives the needed recording space. Y's main advantages are cleaner flip diagrams and not revealing the number of tilings by the number of boards printed.
